paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Ξενοφῶν τὴν τοῦ Σωκράτους ἀπολογίαν διηγεῖται καὶ τὰς αἰτίας προτίθησιν. ὁ κατήγορος φησὶ τὸν Σωκράτη τοὺς μὲν τῆς πόλεως θεοὺς οὐ νομίζειν, καινὰ δὲ δαιμόνια εἰσφέρειν καὶ τοὺς νέους διαφθείρειν. ταῦτα κατηγορίαι εἰσίν, οὐχ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀναγνώστου ἤδη ὁμολογούμενα. πρῶτον οὖν ἀκριβῶς ἀκούσωμεν τί ἕκαστος λέγει, ἔπειτα δὲ πῶς ἀποκρίνεται ὁ Σωκράτης.

Ὁ Σωκράτης ἀποκρίνεται ὅτι τοῖς θεοῖς θύει καὶ ἐν τοῖς κοινοῖς ἱεροῖς. λέγει δὲ πολλοὺς αὐτὸν θύοντα ἑωρακέναι. οὐκ ἀρκεῖ μόνον φάναι «θεοὺς νομίζω», ἀλλὰ τὰ ἔργα μάρτυρας παρέχει. περὶ δὲ τοῦ δαιμονίου σημεῖου τὴν μαντικὴν παραβάλλει. καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι γὰρ διὰ φωνῶν καὶ ὀρνίθων σημεῖα παρὰ τῶν θεῶν ζητοῦσιν.

Ὁ μὲν κατήγορος καινὰ εἰσφέρειν αὐτὸν λέγει, ὁ δὲ Σωκράτης τὴν ἑαυτοῦ πρᾶξιν ταῖς τῶν ἄλλων συγκρίνει. ἐνταῦθα δεῖ τὸν ἀναγνώστην δύο φωνὰς διακρίνειν. ὁ Ξενοφῶν γράφει ὅτι ὁ Σωκράτης φησὶ τοὺς θεοὺς αὐτῷ σημαίνειν. ὁ συγγραφεὺς τὸν λόγον παραδίδωσιν· ὁ Σωκράτης τὴν ἀπόκρισιν ποιεῖται· οἱ θεοὶ τῆς ἐν τῇ ἀποκρίσει πράξεως ὑποκείμενόν εἰσιν.

Περὶ δὲ τῶν νέων ὁ Σωκράτης τὸν Μέλητον ἐρωτᾷ. φησὶ δεῖν δηλοῦν τίνα αὐτὸς ἐκ χρηστοῦ πονηρὸν πεποίηκεν. οὐ γὰρ τὴν συνουσίαν μόνον ἀλλὰ τὴν βλάβην ἀποδεικτέον εἶναι. ὁ δὲ Μέλητος λέγει τοὺς νέους αὐτῷ μᾶλλον πείθεσθαι ἢ τοῖς γονεῦσιν. ὁ Σωκράτης οὖν περὶ παιδείας καὶ ἐπιστήμης ἀποκρίνεται, οὐ τὴν ἐρώτησιν σιωπῇ παρέρχεται.

Ὅταν γὰρ περὶ ὑγιείας ζητῶμεν, τῷ ἰατρῷ πειθόμεθα· περὶ δὲ πορείας τῷ τὴν ὁδὸν ἐπισταμένῳ. οὐ διὰ τοῦτο τοὺς γονέας ἀτιμάζομεν. οὕτως ὁ Σωκράτης ἀξιοῖ τὴν παιδείαν κρίνεσθαι. ὁ δὲ ἀναγνώστης ἐξετάζει εἰ τὸ παράδειγμα πάντα τὰ περὶ τῶν νέων λύει. τὸν λόγον πιστῶς ἀναφέρειν δεῖ, καὶ ὅταν μὴ πάντα αὐτῷ συγχωρῶμεν.

Οἱ δικασταὶ οὐ πάντες πείθονται, καὶ ὁ Σωκράτης κατακρίνεται. ὁ Ξενοφῶν διηγεῖται ὅτι ὁ ἀνὴρ οὐκ ἐθέλει τιμὴν ἑαυτῷ θανάτου ἀντιτιμᾶσθαι· νομίζει γὰρ τοῦτο ὁμολογίαν ἀδικίας εἶναι. τὸν τοῦ Ξενοφῶντος λόγον ἐνταῦθα ἀναγινώσκομεν. ἄλλα βιβλία ἄλλους λόγους παραδίδωσιν, καὶ οὐ δεῖ αὐτοὺς εἰς μίαν ἀπολογίαν ἄνευ σημείου συνάπτειν.

Οἱ φίλοι λυποῦνται, ὁ δὲ Σωκράτης τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γνώμην διαφυλάττει. ὁ συγγραφεὺς δείκνυσιν αὐτὸν οὐ τὸ ζῆν μόνον ἀλλὰ τὸ καλῶς ζῆν προτιμῶντα. ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸν λόγον ἀναφέροντες μὴ λανθάνωμεν τὸν ἀκούοντα περὶ τοῦ τίς λέγει. ὁ κατήγορος αἰτιᾶται, ὁ Σωκράτης ἀποκρίνεται, ὁ Ξενοφῶν ἐξηγεῖται, ὁ δὲ ἀναγνώστης κρίνει. ἐν τούτῳ καὶ ἡ γραμματικὴ καὶ ἡ δικαιοσύνη ἀκρίβειαν αἰτοῦσιν.

reading.translation:
Xenophon narrates Socrates’ defense and sets out the accusations. The accuser says that Socrates does not acknowledge the city’s gods, introduces new divine things, and corrupts the young. These are accusations, not matters already accepted by the reader. Let us therefore first hear precisely what each person says, and then how Socrates replies.

Socrates replies that he sacrifices to the gods, including at public sanctuaries. He says that many have seen him sacrificing. He does not merely say “I acknowledge gods,” but supplies deeds as witnesses. Concerning the divine sign, he draws a comparison with divination. Other people too seek signs from the gods through voices and birds.

The accuser says that he introduces novelties, while Socrates compares his own practice with that of others. Here the reader must distinguish two voices. Xenophon writes that Socrates says that the gods give him signs. The writer transmits the account; Socrates makes the response; the gods are the subject of the action within that response.

Concerning the young, Socrates questions Meletus. He says that it must be made clear whom he has turned from good to bad. The harm, not simply the association, must be demonstrated. Meletus says that the young obey Socrates more than their parents. Socrates therefore responds about education and expertise; he does not pass over the question in silence.

Whenever we investigate health, we obey the doctor; concerning a journey, we follow someone who knows the road. We do not thereby dishonor our parents. Socrates asks that education be judged in this way. The reader examines whether the example resolves every question concerning the young. We must report the argument faithfully even when we do not concede everything to it.

Not all the jurors are persuaded, and Socrates is convicted. Xenophon relates that Socrates is unwilling to propose a counterpenalty in place of death: he considers this an admission of wrongdoing. We are reading Xenophon’s account here. Other works transmit other speeches, and we should not join them into a single defense without indicating the change.

The friends grieve, but Socrates maintains his own judgment. The writer depicts him as preferring not merely living but living well. When we report the argument, let us not leave the listener unaware of who is speaking. The accuser alleges, Socrates replies, Xenophon explains, and the reader judges. Here both grammar and justice demand precision.

sections.title: 1. Mapping a sustained primary-sequence report
body: Begin with the governing verb: λέγει, φησί, γράφει, or a future reporting verb. Mark the boundary of each report before translating. In ὁ Ξενοφῶν γράφει ὅτι ὁ Σωκράτης φησὶ τοὺς θεοὺς σημαίνειν, there are three levels: Xenophon writes; Socrates says; the gods give signs. Each verb has its own subject.

Primary sequence normally preserves the indicative in a finite statement and the subjunctive in an original deliberative or appropriate subordinate clause. The reporting verb’s present tense does not make every embedded action present: λέγει ὅτι ἔθυσεν reports a prior sacrifice. Work from the outer frame inward, then translate the whole thought in natural English.

γράφει ὅτι ὁ Σωκράτης φησὶ τοὺς θεοὺς σημαίνειν.
He writes that Socrates says the gods give signs; nested report.
ἐρωτᾷ τί ποιήσῃ.
He asks what he should do; indirect deliberation.
γράψει ὅτι ἔθυσεν.

sections.title: 2. Relative time in nonfinite reports
body: Under a reporting verb, distinguish simultaneous, prior, subsequent, and perfect-result relations. φησὶ θύειν, θῦσαι, θύσειν, τεθυκέναι can report “is sacrificing,” “sacrificed,” “will sacrifice,” and “has sacrificed.” The future infinitive retains its future relation even if the report is made now.

A perception participle follows its own governing construction. πολλοὺς αὐτὸν θύοντα ἑωρακέναι means that many have seen him sacrificing: πολλούς is the subject of “have seen,” αὐτόν the person seen, and θύοντα agrees with αὐτόν. Do not flatten all accusatives into objects of the outermost verb.

sections.title: 3. Pronouns and the scope of negation
body: A report can change the person of pronouns while retaining the identity of their referents. Direct “I acknowledge gods” may become “Socrates says that he acknowledges gods.” If several men are present, English “he” may be less clear than a repeated name. Greek reflexives can point back to the reporting subject; ordinary pronouns require contextual resolution.

Negation also has scope. οὐ λέγει ὅτι ἀδικεῖ denies that he makes the statement; λέγει ὅτι οὐκ ἀδικεῖ reports a denial of wrongdoing. οὔ φησιν ἀδικεῖν commonly has the latter sense through negative raising. Read the governing construction and the argument rather than moving οὐ mechanically.

table.title: 3. Pronouns and the scope of negation
rows: λέγει ὅτι οὐκ ἀδικεῖ.
He says that he does not do wrong; embedded denial.
οὐ λέγει ὅτι ἀδικεῖ.
He does not say that he does wrong; denial of reporting.
οὔ φησιν ἀδικεῖν.
He denies doing wrong; normal negative-raising reading.
ὁ Σωκράτης λέγει ὅτι αὐτὸς θύει.
Socrates says that he himself sacrifices; explicit reference.
αὐτός / ἑαυτόν
ordinary intensive/pronominal form / reflexive accusative

sections.title: 4. Subordinate clauses inside reports
body: A report may contain a purpose, condition, relative, or question. Bracket it before translating: λέγει ὅτι, ἐὰν οἱ νέοι μανθάνωσιν, βελτίους ἔσονται. The condition belongs to the reported claim, while the outer ὅτι introduces that claim. Its subjunctive is licensed by ἐάν, not by the outer verb λέγει.

Build an annotation with four fields: speaker, governing verb, clause type, and time/aspect. Then produce a faithful connected translation. In a longer passage, follow repeated nouns and pronouns across paragraph boundaries. A fair report can be followed by criticism; do not rewrite a speaker’s position merely to make it easier to reject.

table.title: 4. Subordinate clauses inside reports
rows: λέγει ὅτι ἐὰν μανθάνωσιν, βελτίους ἔσονται.
He says that if they learn, they will be better; embedded condition.
λέγει ὅτι διδάσκει ἵνα μανθάνωσιν.
He says that he teaches so that they may learn; embedded purpose.
λέγει ὅτι οἱ νέοι οὓς διδάσκει ἀκούουσιν.
He says that the young people whom he teaches listen; embedded relative.
ἐρωτᾷ εἰ οἱ νέοι μανθάνουσιν.
He asks whether the young people learn; indirect question.
ἐάν → μανθάνωσιν
the conditional conjunction licenses the subjunctive

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Apology
body: Xenophon’s Apology of Socrates is a short defense of the philosopher’s conduct at his trial in Athens in 399 BCE. “Apology” here means a defense, not an expression of regret. The work opens by asking why Socrates spoke with such elevated self-confidence. Xenophon wants the reader to understand the intention behind that manner, including Socrates’ judgment about his age, life, and approaching death. The choice of opening question shapes everything that follows.

The work moves from a conversation with Hermogenes before the trial to selected courtroom exchanges, reactions, the verdict, and Socrates’ response. It does not attempt to reproduce every procedural stage or every word spoken. Xenophon explicitly names Hermogenes as an informant in section 2. That is valuable evidence about a chain of testimony, but it does not turn the finished literary work into a transcript. Ask when the narrator summarizes, when Socrates answers an objection, and when a friend’s report supplies the connection.

Plato wrote a different Apology, and the two works should be read as distinct presentations. Do not silently import Plato’s famous phrases or penalty proposals into Xenophon’s account. Xenophon also defends Socrates across the four books of the Memorabilia, where conversations and habits provide a broader portrait. Read sections 1–9 for the preparation, 10–26 for the selected trial account, and the closing sections for the remembered aftermath. The complete translation linked here makes it possible to see the lesson’s excerpt in its argumentative setting. Across Lessons 45–47, notice how preparation, reputation, and courtroom reporting each illuminate a different part of Xenophon’s purpose.

sections.title: A literary defense and a civic trial
body: Separate prosecution, defense, verdict, and penalty. Xenophon selects exchanges that support his interpretation of Socrates’ manner. A literary defense is not a verbatim transcript, even when it presents direct speech. Keep Xenophon’s account internally consistent before comparing it with Plato’s different Apology.

Athenian citizen jurors heard speeches and voted. The institutions differed from a modern courtroom; do not supply a modern judge, jury deliberation scene, or gavel merely because they are familiar. The banner is a cautious reconstruction rather than evidence for the exact arrangement of Socrates’ trial.

sections.title: The death of Socrates: what happened
body: Socrates was executed at Athens in 399 BCE after his conviction. Plato’s Phaedo supplies the principal detailed literary account of his final day. Its opening explains that execution was delayed during Athens’ sacred mission to Delos. Friends then spend the final day with him in prison, discussing philosophy and the soul.

At the end, Socrates drinks the poison traditionally identified as hemlock, walks as instructed, and lies down when his legs grow heavy. The attendant examines the loss of sensation and the spreading coldness. Socrates’ final request concerns a cock owed to Asclepius; Crito closes his eyes and mouth after death. The meaning of that offering remains debated. Read the scene as Plato’s carefully shaped account, not a modern clinical report.

sections.title: Where it is recorded
body: Read Phaedo 57a–59c for the narrative frame, delay, and companions, and 115a–118a for the preparations and death. Phaedo recounts the day to Echecrates; at 59b, Plato is said to have been ill and absent. The dialogue presents eyewitness testimony through a literary frame rather than claiming that Plato himself watched the event.

Plato’s Apology concerns the trial, while the Crito stages the argument about escaping from prison. The Phaedo is the work to consult for the final conversation and death. Xenophon’s Apology and Memorabilia provide a different defense and remembrance of Socrates; do not transfer Plato’s arguments for immortality to Xenophon.

sections.title: How Xenophon might have learned
body: Xenophon was away from Athens and did not witness the execution. In Apology 2 and Memorabilia 4.8.4 he explicitly identifies Hermogenes as an informant about Socrates’ attitude and preparation. Plato also lists Hermogenes among the companions present on the final day at Phaedo 59b. This gives us a documented connection to someone represented as close to the events.

We do not know who first brought Xenophon news of the death, precisely where he received it, or when that first report reached him. Travelers, fellow soldiers, letters, and conversations with friends are plausible channels, but no particular messenger, letter, or scene should be narrated as established fact. Distinguish the attested informant from the uncertain first arrival of the news.

sections.title: Looking closely: David’s The Death of Socrates
body: Jacques-Louis David painted The Death of Socrates in 1787, more than two thousand years after the execution. Socrates reaches for the cup while raising his other hand; he is not shown already drinking. His composure contrasts with the grief around him. The full painting is reproduced below so that these relationships remain visible.

The seated Plato at the foot of the bed represents the author who preserved the story. His inclusion is an artistic choice, not proof of his attendance: the Phaedo itself says he was absent. Compare two details with the text and identify one departure or interpretive choice. Treat the painting as an eighteenth-century interpretation of philosophical courage, not an ancient eyewitness image.

sections.title: Translate, attribute, and compare
body: Translate the complete Greek reading in connected English, marking where the accuser’s allegation ends and Socrates’ answer begins. In one nested sentence, label the writer, reported speaker, and actor. Then explain why reporting a claim accurately does not require agreeing with it.

For the Culture/History response, write three labeled statements: what Plato narrates, what Xenophon documents about an informant, and what remains inference. Use the painting to explain how later remembrance can add meaning without adding historical evidence. This prepares the final lesson’s comparison of a remembered life and civic justice.
